aliases.name: 6,5 x 51 R (Arisaka)
aliases.note: The C.I.P. designation, which measures the case at 51 mm rather than 50 mm.

aliases.name: Type 38 cartridge
aliases.note: The 1907 spitzer version, which is the load recorded on this page.

bulletDiameter.sourceNote: Cartridge maximum, dimension G1, and the same figure the encyclopedia infobox gives. The lead sentence of that article instead states 6.705 mm, which the datasheet contradicts.

caseLength.sourceNote: Cartridge maximum, dimension L3. C.I.P. names the round after this figure; the common name rounds it down to 50 mm.

rimDiameter.sourceNote: Dimension R1. It stands 0.63 mm proud of the base, which is what makes the case semi-rimmed rather than rimmed or rimless.

maxPressure.sourceNote: Pmax 2950 bar. This is the modern commercial ceiling, not an Imperial Japanese Army specification.

bulletMass.sourceNote: 138.9 gr as published in the article's ballistics table, converted to grams; the article's running text gives the same bullet as 9.0 g.

barrelLength.sourceNote: Test barrel length stated for the ballistics table: 800 mm, which is close to the Type 38 rifle's own barrel.

velocity.sourceNote: 770 m/s as published, in an infobox that declares SI ballistics.

images.alt: Three bottlenecked brass rifle cartridges standing on a wooden table beside a steel rule marked in millimetres and inches. The middle one is markedly slimmer than the other two and carries a lead-tipped copper bullet; the left has a wider body and a blunter bullet; the right is the tallest, with a jacketed bullet showing a cannelure.
images.caption: .303 British on the left, 6.5x50mmSR Arisaka in the centre and .30-06 Springfield on the right, against a millimetre rule. The Japanese round is the slenderest of the three, and the comparison is the one its critics kept making.

images.alt: A grey-toned technical drawing of three sectioned cartridges. The tall one on the left, labelled “Ball”, shows a pointed jacketed bullet seated in a case, with a line pointing to a “pink band” at the case mouth. A shorter one in the centre, labelled “Practice”, has callouts reading copper jacket, lead core and wool fibre. On the right, labelled “Wood”, a case carries a long tapered wooden projectile.
images.caption: Sectioned drawings of three Type 38 rounds from a United States Army and Air Force intelligence manual on Japanese ammunition: the ball round, a practice round with a partly hollow bullet, and a wooden-bulleted blank. The ball round's callout marks a pink band at the case mouth.
